raised.claim: parseScopeBlock takes the FIRST ```triage-scope match in the issue body, but the created body is model-authored `issue.body` followed by our rendered block — so a fence inside the model's body silently becomes the enforced scope, defeating the "we parse our own output" guarantee.

The tool schema types `col`/`op` as free strings and `value` as ['string','number','null'], which is strictly looser than ScopeTermSchema — a payload that passes generation-time validation can fail AnalysisSchema.parse and kill the whole run's batch.
raised.why_it_breaks: Strict tool use validates the JSON schema, which accepts `{col:'candidates_count', op:'==', value:0}` (typo'd op), `{col:'style', op:'=', value:1}` (numeric op on a nullable col), `{col:'candidates_count', op:'=', value:null}` (the schema's own comment tells the model `value` may be null), or `{col:'source_url', op:'contains', value:''}`. Every one of these fails the zod union (numeric variant needs `value: z.number()`, contains needs `z.string().min(1)`, unknown col matches no variant), so the entire Analysis fails to parse, the catch in orphan-triage treats it as a non-transient error and `finish()` closes the Warsaw day — 50 orphans wait until tomorrow and the run's LLM cost is burned over one malformed scope term. This contradicts the file's own stated intent that zod stay lenient so a bad optional field "parses as 'unproven' instead of failing the whole batch".

raised.claim: The saturation guard compares every verdict in the batch against a single pre-run snapshot of postCreationRows and never increments it as verdicts are pushed, so one run can attach arbitrarily more than MAX_ROWS_PER_ISSUE rows to the same issue.
raised.why_it_breaks: `postCreationRows` is computed once per issue at plan time (countRowsForIssue before any writes). If an issue sits at 11 rows and the batch contains 50 verdicts naming it, all 50 pass the `>= 12` check and are pushed via `pushInto(byIssue, ...)`, leaving the issue at 61 rows. The magnet shape (#347: 36 rows) can therefore be recreated in a single day, which is precisely what guard 4 exists to prevent.

raised.claim: Guard-3 degraded verdicts are written as `matcher_bug` but land in the `plan.quiet` loop's `else` branch, so the daily digest counts them as `wontfix` — a terminal class they explicitly are not.
raised.why_it_breaks: planTriageActions pushes `{ ...verdict, review_class: 'matcher_bug', ... }` into `quiet` when the absence claim has no probe evidence. The job then does `if (v.review_class === 'not_on_untappd') notOnUntappd++ else wontfix++`, so a run where 5 rows are degraded reports "5 wontfix" in the digest line while the rows are matcher_bug and still in the enrichment/retry pool. An operator reading the digest concludes 5 rows were closed as unfixable when they are actually pending retry.

raised.claim: countRowsForIssue compares `reviewed_at` (written as JS `toISOString()`, millisecond precision) against GitHub's `created_at` (second precision), and `nowIso` is captured at run START while the issue is created LATER in the same run — so rows attached in the run that created an issue are permanently excluded from the count, and same-second rows are mis-compared as strings.
raised.why_it_breaks: `nowIso = now.toISOString()` yields `2026-08-14T10:00:00.123Z`; GitHub returns `created_at: '2026-08-14T10:00:00Z'`. SQLite compares TEXT lexicographically, and '.' < 'Z', so `reviewed_at > createdAt` is false for every row reviewed in the same second as creation. Since the createIssue → `review(v, number)` sequence writes all creation-cohort rows with the run-start `nowIso`, which is EARLIER than the wall-clock instant GitHub stamps, an issue born carrying 12 rows reads postCreationRows = 0 forever and accepts 12 more before the guard engages. The saturation threshold is effectively off by the size of the creation batch.

raised.claim: guardHits is only surfaced on the `covered < orphans.length` shortfall branch, but `covered` counts verdicts before any guard runs — so a batch where every row got a verdict that the guards then rejected logs no guardHits line at all, exactly the "model looping on one illegal proposal" case the log line was added for.
raised.why_it_breaks: `covered` is `new Set(analysis.verdicts.map(v => v.beer_id).filter(id => byId.has(id))).size` — it ignores whether planTriageActions skipped the verdict. Feed a 5-row batch where the model returns 5 verdicts each pointing at a new_issue whose `where` is review_class-only: all 5 are dropped by guard 1 (illegal_scope = 5), covered = 5 = orphans.length, so `log.warn({ ..., guardHits: plan.guardHits }, ...)` never executes. The only trace is `outcome.skipped` in the digest, with no reason attached.

raised.quote:
reviewed_at        = CASE
         WHEN (enrich_failures.candidates_count = 0) <> (excluded.candidates_count = 0)
         THEN NULL ELSE enrich_failures.reviewed_at END`,
raised.claim: recordEnrichFailure's re-open branch clears review_class/review_note/reviewed_at on the 0↔>0 candidates boundary but leaves the new `issue_number` column set, so a re-opened row keeps a stale issue link.
raised.why_it_breaks: A row attached to #408 (issue_number = 408) whose next failure flips candidates_count across the zero boundary gets review_class/reviewed_at = NULL (it re-enters the untriaged pool) while issue_number stays 408. Any audit query "which rows went to #408" now returns a row that is not triaged to it, and if the row is later re-triaged quietly (`review(v, null)`) or left untriaged it keeps pointing at the wrong issue. The new column should follow the same lifecycle as reviewed_at in this CASE.

raised.quote:
if (!allowedKeys.has(verdict.new_issue_key!)) { skipped++; continue; }
      pushInto(byKey, verdict.new_issue_key!, verdict);
raised.claim: Verdicts routed to a NEW issue via new_issue_key are never checked against that issue's own scope (rowSatisfiesScope / isLegalScope only run for existing issues and for the proposal's legality), so a model can file rows that contradict the scope the issue is created with.
raised.why_it_breaks: The model submits `new_issues: [{key:'k1', scope:{beer_ids:[], where:[{col:'candidates_count',op:'>',value:0}]}}]` and attaches verdicts for rows with candidates_count = 0 to k1. planTriageActions pushes them all, the issue is created with a scope that provably contradicts its own first cohort, and those rows get issue_number = k1's number. Tomorrow an identical zero-candidate row is rejected by guard 2 as a scope_violation while its sibling sits inside the issue — the invariant "no consequence applied without evidence from the row itself" holds for comments but not for creation.

raised.claim: isLegalScope is applied only to proposed new issues; an EXISTING issue whose parsed scope is a whole-class `where: [review_class = X]` is still honored by guard 2, so the #347 dumping-ground shape can re-enter through an existing issue's body (or the upcoming manual backfill).
raised.why_it_breaks: Guard 2 checks only `target.scope === null || !rowSatisfiesScope(...)`. If the ops backfill (or anyone editing an issue body) writes a `triage-scope` block of `{"beer_ids":[],"where":[{"col":"review_class","op":"=","value":"matcher_bug"}]}`, parseScopeBlock returns it, rowSatisfiesScope accepts every matcher_bug row (review_class is matched against the verdict), and the issue becomes an unbounded class magnet again — with guard 1 raising no counter because it never runs on existing issues. Illegal scope should be rejected at parse/use time, not only at proposal time.

raised.claim: The scope block is appended to the END of the created issue body but the prompt renders only `body.slice(0, 2000)`, so an issue whose model-authored body is long loses its scope block from the prompt and the model cannot see what the issue covers.
raised.why_it_breaks: `body = `${issue.body}\n\n${renderScopeBlock(issue.scope)}`` puts the block last; a 2500-char body (body is `z.string().min(1)`, uncapped) means the next run's prompt shows none of the scope. The model then proposes attachments for rows the guard will reject (scope_violation → skipped, no re-routing), producing a silent backlog churn for that issue with no signal in the prompt that the constraint exists.

raised.quote: SET issue_number = CAST(substr(review_note, instr(review_note, '→ #') + 3) AS INTEGER)
raised.claim: The v23 backfill keys on the FIRST '→ #' anywhere in review_note, so a note whose model-authored text already contains an arrow reference gets the wrong issue number backfilled.
raised.why_it_breaks: review_note is model text (`z.string().min(1).max(500)`) and the job appends the suffix as `${v.review_note} → #${issueNumber}`. A legacy note like 'alias gap → #228 per earlier note → #347' resolves via instr to the FIRST occurrence, so issue_number becomes 228 instead of 347 — a wrong row→issue link in the one-time backfill that nothing re-checks. Anchoring on the last occurrence (or on the trailing suffix) would be safe; instr's first match is not.

raised.claim: Guard 3 accepts a single empty probe channel as full proof of absence, but the prompt's own evidence rules treat a name-probe hit under another brewery as a brewery-label (matcher) problem, not as absence.
raised.why_it_breaks: If the brewery probe returns '' while the name probe returns 'Mad Elf, MadTree' — i.e. the beer name DOES exist on Untappd, just under a different brewery — `proved` is true via `probe?.brewery === ''`, so a not_on_untappd verdict survives and the row is terminally closed, while the prompt says "a beer found under a DIFFERENT brewery is a brewery-label problem". The test that pins the opposite case ('a probe that returned hits is not absence evidence') only covers BOTH channels non-empty, so this half is untested.
